vignette:
He works late nights now, long after the office empties. The tax consultancy firm is quiet, fluorescent lights humming over rows of empty desks, and he tells himself it is safer this way-fewer people, fewer eyes. He is eighteen, the youngest in his department, and his colleagues call him diligent. They do not know that he cannot bear the crowded morning commute, the press of bodies against his back, the way a stranger's elbow brushing his shoulder makes his breath catch and his hands go cold.

He remembers the night with a clarity that feels like betrayal. It was three months ago, after a party hosted by someone he thought was a friend. He had drunk too much, maybe, but he remembers the walk home through the dim streets of his neighborhood in Lagos. He remembers the shortcut he took through the unfinished building, the way the gravel shifted under his feet. Then the hands, the voice, the weight of another man's body pinning him to the damp concrete floor. He remembers the smell of dust and sweat and something metallic, and the sound of his own voice breaking into a plea that went unheard. He remembers nothing after that until he woke on his own bed, clothes torn, bruises blooming on his thighs, and a silence so heavy it pressed the air out of his lungs.

He did not tell anyone. Not his mother, who would have cried and asked too many questions. Not his pastor, who would have spoken of forgiveness. He told no one, and he washed himself three times that morning, scrubbing until his skin was raw, and then he put on a clean shirt and went to work. The tax consultant job had been a miracle-a cousin's connection, a chance to escape the cycle of poverty. He could not afford to lose it.

Now, every day is a negotiation with the past. At his desk, he reviews client returns, but the columns of numbers blur and shift. He sees the face of the man instead of the figures, hears the gravelly whisper beneath the hum of the air conditioner. He jolts when a file drops, heart hammering. His supervisor once tapped him on the shoulder to hand him a report, and he swung around with a fist raised, face white. He apologized quickly, said he had not slept well. The supervisor laughed it off. He does not laugh anymore himself. He cannot remember the last time he laughed.

He avoids people now. The lunchroom chatter grates, and when a female colleague teases him about being quiet, he feels a surge of anger so sudden and hot it frightens him. He does not understand where the anger comes from. He has always been a calm boy, a good son, a hard worker. Now he is a stranger to himself. He snaps at clients who ask questions. He forgets meetings. He starts at every shadow.

At night, the dreams come. Not always of the event itself-sometimes just the feeling of being trapped, of a weight on his chest, of hands where hands should not be. He wakes gasping, drenched, and then lies still, counting the cracks in the ceiling until dawn. He has stopped sleeping in his own room. He sleeps on the sofa, where the door is in view. He checks the lock three times before closing his eyes. He never lets his back face the door.

There is a shame that lives inside him, a voice that whispers he invited it, that he should have fought harder, that he is less than a man now. He has not told a soul. He cannot. The words would turn to stone in his throat. So he carries the silence like a second skin, and he goes to work, and he fills out forms, and he adds columns of numbers that never quite balance. He wonders if anything will ever balance again.
